country.name: Luxembourg
country.tagline: Forty kilometres of Moselle riverbank where Crémant, Riesling and Auxerrois face Germany across the water.

stats.note: About 1,295 ha per Wikipedia (de) Weinbau in Luxemburg; production in recent years has been roughly 0.1 mhl but no 2025 figure was found.

country.overview:
Luxembourg's wine country is a single strip of slopes along the left bank of the Moselle, about 42 km from Schengen in the south to Wasserbillig and Rosport in the north, facing Germany's Obermosel on the opposite bank. Roughly 1,300 hectares of vines are farmed by about 450 growers, and the whole country is one appellation, the AOP Moselle Luxembourgeoise.

The wines are mostly dry whites from grapes that like cool, limestone country: Rivaner (Müller-Thurgau), Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling and the ancient Elbling, plus Gewürztraminer and a growing share of Pinot Noir. Sparkling wine is the country's great success. Crémant de Luxembourg, created on 4 January 1991 for traditional-method wines, accounts for a large share of sales, and houses such as Bernard-Massard in Grevenmacher have made sparkling wine since the 1920s.

The southern half, the canton of Remich, has softer limestone and marl soils and gives rounder wines; the northern half around Grevenmacher and Wormeldange has steeper slopes of shell limestone (Muschelkalk) and gives Luxembourg's best Rieslings, notably from the Koeppchen above Wormeldange. Cooperatives (Domaines Vinsmoselle) produce well over half the wine, private growers about a quarter, and the trade the rest. The village of Schengen, where the 1985 agreement on open borders was signed on a riverboat, is the southern gateway of the wine route.

history.title: Romans on the Moselle
history.text: Roman settlers planted vines on the Moselle, part of the same wine economy that supplied Trier.

history.title: Elbling after the great frost
history.text: After the catastrophic winter of 1709 about 90 percent of replanting was Elbling, sold in bulk to German Mosel blenders for two centuries.

history.title: A national quality push
history.text: After the end of the customs union with Germany, Luxembourg replaced Elbling with better varieties, founded the Institut viti-vinicole in Remich (1925) and created the Marque Nationale (12 March 1935).

history.title: Crémant de Luxembourg
history.text: Crémant de Luxembourg was introduced on 4 January 1991 for traditional-method sparkling wine.

history.title: AOP reform
history.text: The old Vin classé, Premier Cru and Grand Premier Cru tasting grades were dropped in favour of an origin pyramid: Côtes de, Coteaux de and Lieu-dit.

country.classification: One PDO, Moselle Luxembourgeoise (registered 1973), covering 12 communes. Since the 2014 reform labels use three tiers of origin: 'Côtes de' plus a village (approachable everyday wines), 'Coteaux de' plus a broader terroir (premium wines from defined limestone or marl zones) and 'Lieu-dit' plus a named site (single-vineyard wines with lower yields). Crémant de Luxembourg is a sparkling style within the AOP. The Marque Nationale label (since 1935) certifies wines made from Luxembourg grapes and controlled by the state.
country.climate_soils: A cool, temperate climate moderated by the Moselle. In the south (canton of Remich) Keuper marl and gypsum give rounder, softer wines; in the north (canton of Grevenmacher) the slopes are steeper and made of shell limestone (Muschelkalk), giving more tension and structure, especially in Riesling.

grapes.name: Rivaner (Müller-Thurgau)
grapes.note: The most planted grape, for easy everyday whites.

grapes.name: Auxerrois
grapes.note: A Luxembourg speciality, soft and creamy, often the base of Crémant.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc
grapes.note: Important for still wine and Crémant.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Best on the shell limestone of the north.

grapes.name: Elbling
grapes.note: The ancient Moselle grape, light and tart.

regions.name: Moselle Luxembourgeoise
regions.tagline: One river, one appellation, and a sparkling-wine country in miniature.
regions.summary: The Luxembourg Moselle runs from Schengen to Wasserbillig along a 42 km wine route, with villages such as Remerschen, Wellenstein, Remich, Stadtbredimus, Ehnen, Wormeldange, Machtum and Grevenmacher. Riesling, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Rivaner dominate, and Crémant is the national pride.
regions.history: Roman, then monastic, then a bulk Elbling supplier to Germany, Luxembourg rebuilt its wine identity after 1919, with the Institut viti-vinicole at Remich and the Marque Nationale in 1935. The cooperative movement (Domaines Vinsmoselle) dominates production; private growers such as Alice Hartmann, Domaine Thill, Schumacher-Knepper and Abi Duhr's Château Pauqué lead quality.
regions.terroir: Keuper marl in the south, Muschelkalk in the north; south-east-facing slopes above the river.
regions.grapes: Rivaner, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Elbling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Dry whites, Crémant, some reds and late-harvest wines.
regions.classification: AOP Moselle Luxembourgeoise with Côtes de, Coteaux de and Lieu-dit levels; Crémant de Luxembourg.

lu-moselle-luxembourgeoise.name: Moselle Luxembourgeoise
lu-moselle-luxembourgeoise.grapes: Rivaner, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Elbling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Saint Laurent
lu-moselle-luxembourgeoise.summary: Luxembourg's single wine PDO covers the 12 Moselle communes from Schengen to Rosport. Since 2014 it has worked as an origin pyramid: Côtes de (village wines), Coteaux de (premium terroir zones) and Lieu-dit (single vineyards such as Wormeldinger Koeppchen). Dry whites are the norm, and Crémant de Luxembourg, defined in 1991, is the commercial engine. Notable sites include the Koeppchen (Wormeldange), Primerberg (Remerschen), Göllebour (Remich) and the Fels at Grevenmacher.
lu-moselle-luxembourgeoise.terroir: Marl and gypsum in the south, steep shell limestone in the north, all moderated by the Moselle.
lu-moselle-luxembourgeoise.nerd_note: The EU register allows a theoretical maximum yield of 140 hl/ha for the AOP base level, but Lieu-dit wines are held to much lower yields.

sites.name: Wormeldinger Koeppchen
sites.text: A steep shell-limestone slope above Wormeldange crowned by a chapel, Luxembourg's most famous Riesling vineyard.

sites.name: Musée du Vin, Ehnen
sites.text: A wine-growers' house in the village of Ehnen, now a museum of Moselle viticulture with old presses and a vineyard.

sites.name: Caves Bernard-Massard
sites.text: Grevenmacher's leading sparkling-wine house, with cellars tunnelled into the hillside and one of the largest Crémant productions in Luxembourg.

sites.name: Institut viti-vinicole, Remich
sites.text: The state institute in Remich that analyses every Luxembourg wine, runs the Marque Nationale and does vine research.

sites.name: Schengen
sites.class: Southern gateway of the wine route
sites.text: The wine village at the meeting point of Luxembourg, Germany and France where the Schengen Agreement was signed on a Moselle riverboat in 1985; its castle estate is home to Domaine Thill.
